Pele Yoetz 27:6: And they have already said in the Talmud (Sotah 22a): we learned fear of sin from a maiden - for Rabbi Yochanan heard that maiden praying: Master of the universe, You created the Garden of Eden, You created Gehinnom, You created the righteous, You created the wicked. May it be Your will, O LORD our God and God of our fathers, that men not stumble because of me. So should all maidens conduct themselves and be hidden - "all the glory of the king's daughter is within" (Psalms 45:14), she shall not show herself outside to the eye. And behold, in the cities of Ishmael they are somewhat careful of this, but in the cities of Edom immodesty has multiplied, for such is the custom of these lands - the letters of "minhag" [custom] are those of "Gehinnom." And "a woman who fears the LORD, she shall be praised" (Proverbs 31:30), and she shall not follow the majority to do evil, and her reward shall be doubled and redoubled. And it is written in Sefer Chasidim (385) that a certain young woman would not adorn herself at all, so that those who saw her not stumble because of her, and she merited a fine match - a wise and pious man.
Pele Yoetz 27:7: And the LORD has a grievance with the wealthy of the people, whose hand has attained a vast fortune and who seek to match their daughters with young men of their own set, wealthy like themselves, and open their hand to give a large dowry - money moving by the thousands and tens of thousands - in order to acquire young men who are empty vessels devoid of Torah and fear of the LORD. If only they were wise, they would understand that even if their wealth should rise to the heavens, in the end their bodies are not money, and it is destined to go to ruin - "if you cast but a glance at it, it is gone" - as we have seen with our own eyes how many who at the time of their marriage were exceedingly wealthy lost that wealth and came to wander for bread. And even while he remains wealthy, that woman shall live a life of hardship, for mostly her husband is not with her, but travels the roads, the seas, and the rivers, and is always occupied with his workers and his accounts, and "he who increases possessions increases worry" (Avot 2:7), rising early and staying up late, eating the bread of sorrows (Psalms 127:2) - and since he is preoccupied and irritable, he increases quarrels with his wife over nothing. And her distress shall be all the greater if she fears the LORD and sees that her husband has no fear of Heaven and is not careful with mitzvot, as is the custom of many of the common people, so that all her days are filled with pain. Not so one who gives his daughter to a Torah scholar - how good is her portion and how pleasant is her lot and his lot in this world and in the World to Come, and all the days of her life she shall live in peace of mind and find honor and shall not lack for provision.
Pele Yoetz 27:8: And if daughters and their fathers thought about the great peace of mind and the good that a Torah scholar's wife and her father have in this world and in the World to Come, they would give their very souls and their money for this, and even if she should be sustained by charity, it would be no disgrace to them, for great is the honor accorded to the righteous in the World to Come. And how much more so, in a place where they lavish large dowries on young men of their own set, they could instead enrich the Torah scholar so that he be settled to pursue Torah and service. And it is known, the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Berachot 34b), that all the prophets prophesied only concerning one who marries his daughter to a Torah scholar, who supports those who study Torah.
Pele Yoetz 27:9: And it is true that they are matched in their measure - for even the Torah scholar does not want the daughter of the wealthy, wishing to fulfill the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Yevamot 63a): descend a rung [in social status] to take a wife - and the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Pesachim 49a): let a person always sell all that he has and marry the daughter of a Torah scholar - and one who marries a woman must check her brothers, for most children resemble the mother's brothers (Bava Batra 110a). And if a man gives all the wealth of his house to a Torah scholar out of love for the Holy One, blessed be He, and to fulfill the words of our Sages, of blessed memory, they mock him greatly. But nevertheless, it is already written in Sefer Chasidim (381) that if the Torah scholar is in dire straits and sees that a wealthy man's daughter and her family desire Torah, and they offer him a large dowry in a manner that he can be settled for Torah and service, if he takes her he has not lost - and the LORD shall not withhold from him a holy seed, since he marries for the sake of Heaven (and I shall write more of this under the entry "Zivug" [match]). This is the teaching between a father and his daughter - let the wise man hear and understand still more from his own knowledge.
Pele Yoetz 28:1: Idleness - Idleness is a sick evil, and one who sits idle is called a scoffer, for he mocks the greatness of the reward of Torah, and is like one to whom it is said: count out gold coins from the king's treasury and whatever you count shall be yours - yet he mocks the gold coins and prefers instead to sit idle. And the greatest reward there is in Torah is that it gives peace of mind to its Maker. And whoever does not concern himself with giving peace of mind to his Maker is included among all who have no regard for their Maker's honor, of whom our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Chagigah 11b) that it would have been fitting for him not to have come into the world. Woe to these creatures for the disgrace of the Torah, woe and alas, and hearts ache at seeing the evil of how the sin of the neglect of Torah has become like something permitted. Is it not enough that exile and poverty have left no good trait for Israel, and most of our days and nights we are occupied with our affairs, bringing sustenance to our house and other bodily needs, as though man were born for toil to labor over his bodily needs - it would be fitting for us that when we find a free moment to study or hear teachings, we should grasp it with both hands to give peace of mind to our Former thereby, for this is our portion from all our labor - yet we, sinners against our own souls, even on Sabbaths and festivals choose to sit in the marketplaces and streets, occupied with strolling or idle conversation, and on the long winter nights engage in frivolous merriment and laughter and levity, rather than occupy ourselves with Torah or go to a Torah scholar to hear teachings. Woe to us on the day of judgment and the day of rebuke.
Pele Yoetz 28:2: Brothers and friends, let us be strong and strengthen ourselves, and have mercy on the honor of our Maker and on our own souls, and not destroy ourselves knowingly. Let us come and return to the LORD, and not lose from the precious time even a moment - for let us believe with complete faith that God shall bring everything into judgment, even a brief moment such as it takes to swallow one's own saliva, as they said on the verse (Job 7:19), "You do not let me alone even long enough to swallow my saliva" - and let our own inclination not mislead us with vain and misleading claims (and I shall write more of this under the entry "Torah"), and may the LORD God help us.
Pele Yoetz 29:1: Weeping - There is a time to weep, such as when one prays to the LORD and pours out his conversation, seeking forgiveness through confessions and supplications for sins and transgressions - his heart shall pour out like water and his tears shall fall, and especially during the mighty month of Elul and the Ten Days of Repentance, when "a king establishes the land through judgment" (Proverbs 29:4) - one must come with weeping and supplications. And the virtue of weeping is very great, for they said (Berachot 32b): from the day the Temple was destroyed, the gates of prayer were locked, but the gates of tears were not locked. And they said in the Holy Zohar on the verse (Exodus 2:6), "and she opened it and saw the child, and behold, a youth [na'ar] weeping" - this refers to Israel, as it is written (Hosea 11:1), "for Israel was a youth [na'ar]" - and as soon as they open with weeping, immediately "she had compassion on him." And the disciples of the Ari wrote that the morning prayer should be prayed with joy, and the evening prayer with weeping, and a sign for this is "in the evening weeping lodges, but joy comes in the morning" (Psalms 30:6). But for us, orphans of orphans, would that we prayed all our prayers with weeping. And even though one should serve the LORD with joy and gladness of heart more than anything, nevertheless these should be mixed together - an eye weeping bitterly and a joyful heart - joy on the one hand, for having merited to stand and serve before the King of glory and give peace of mind before the throne of His glory, for there is no joy in the world greater than this, and bitterness in sighing over not knowing how to serve God as required.
Pele Yoetz 29:2: And especially when he takes to heart the words of the prayer he recites - "and graciously grant us from Yourself wisdom, understanding, and knowledge" - let him remember his own limited worth. And when he says "bring us back, our Father," let him also remember that he is far from the LORD. And when he says "forgive us, our Father, for we have sinned," let him remember and let his soul be downcast over having sinned against a high and exalted King, awesome and fearsome. And so, in this manner, if he takes to heart all the blessings and the words of the prayers, he shall find room to be embittered with weeping, and shall pour out his soul in weeping, and "the poor man speaks with supplications" (Proverbs 18:23), anxious yet trusting greatly in the mercy of Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 29:3: And likewise in reciting the confessions, weeping and sighing are needed, inwardly and outwardly, as written under the entry "Vidui" [confession]. And likewise when reciting Tikkun Chatzot, and especially on the Ninth of Av, let him increase weeping, mourning, and lamentation. And likewise over a worthy person who has passed away, causing him grief, he must weep - for they said (Shabbat 105b) that whoever weeps and mourns for a worthy person is forgiven all his sins. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (ibid.) that all the tears a person sheds for the sake of Heaven, as in the matter mentioned and the like, are very precious before the LORD, to the point that He counts them and places them in His treasury. Behold, therefore, let a man gather strength to shed tears like a stream - a thing in its proper time, how good it is.
Pele Yoetz 29:4: And it is true that tears are not bound up in our garments to bring them forth whenever we wish, and how many times we wish to weep a great weeping as is required, and we say, "would that our head were water and our eyes a fountain of tears, that we might weep day and night" - but what shall we do when the doors of our eyes are closed and locked, and not even one tear comes out - and this is because of our own smallness and limited understanding, for we do not know what we lack, nor do we purify our souls, and the eyes of our soul have grown dim from seeing the evil we have caused, and we do not feel the evil in which we find ourselves - and therefore our eyes do not shed streams of water as tears fall of their own accord for a man whose relative has died before him, or who has lost his wealth, and the like. But the pure man, even though he himself does not see it, his fortune does see it, and his tears fall without ceasing. But in any case, let us do what is in our power to do, and press ourselves with many thoughts, as the matter requires, to arouse weeping, for it is within a person's power to bring forth tears by force of will.
Pele Yoetz 29:5: And according to the greatness of the special power of tears, it is fitting to strengthen oneself to bring them forth at their proper time. And if he cannot bring forth a single tear by any means, let him raise his voice in weeping, for this too is valued before the LORD and drives away the accusers, as it is written (Psalms 6:9): "depart from me, all workers of iniquity, for the LORD has heard the voice of my weeping." But in private shall his soul weep, between himself and his Maker, in a manner that people do not come to mock him and it does not appear as arrogance - and everything depends on what kind of person he is and on the place and the time. There is a time when it is fitting to raise a voice of weeping and to weep and cause others to weep, to arouse the people to weeping, and there is a person for whom it is fitting to conceal his weeping - for this is the straight path: "in all your ways" and "walk humbly with your God," and let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven, and "a good man conducts his affairs with judgment" (Psalms 112:5).
Pele Yoetz 29:6: And included in the obligation of weeping is to weep over one's own dead - and needless to say when his soul is bitter over it, for surely he shall weep day and night without ceasing - but even if his soul is not bitter over it, such as one who has many children and had a small child who was sick for a long period, so that the members of the household lived a life of hardship because of him, and it became a very great burden to them, to the point that they could not wait for the time when he would die and they would be relieved of their weary strength; and likewise if it was an old man, advanced in years, who had become a great burden on the members of his household, greatly afflicted with suffering, in a manner that at his death he would go to his rest and give relief to his household - even so, one must be aroused to weeping and weep for him three days, to fulfill the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Mo'ed Katan 27b): "three days for weeping" - let him not add to it, nor detract from it. And needless to say if it is a small child, for whom it is fitting to be aroused to weeping, saying "the fruit of my womb is the sin of my soul" - as is known, that tender children die because of the sin of their father and mother, and it is found that they are the slaughterers of the children, and "God shall bring everything into judgment." And even though there are many ways and many answers and consolations with which comforters may properly comfort - "for He who takes souls is wise, and His designs are established," and similar words from the gates of consolation - nevertheless, for all three days, one should not turn so much to the voice of comforters, but his own flesh shall ache for his dead, and he shall weep bitterly for his own sin, and let his tears pass over his forehead to remove his guilt - and this is his atonement.
Pele Yoetz 29:7: And the brothers and sisters too should properly weep and mourn, as our Sages, of blessed memory, established, taking to heart that if they had been worthy this trouble would not have befallen them - as it is written (Deuteronomy 32:4), "the Rock, His work is perfect" - for the standard of the Holy One, blessed be He, is not like the standard of flesh and blood. The standard of flesh and blood is: if a person is liable to death, even though his father and mother and his brothers and sisters and relatives are innocent, they have no mercy on them or on their distress, but only the sinning soul shall die - but the Holy One, blessed be He, is not so; He does not pain a person for nothing, but rather a person does not die until he himself is liable and his father and mother are liable to the degree of distress they shall suffer, and his wife to the degree of distress she shall suffer, and his brothers and sisters and relatives and acquaintances to the degree of distress they shall suffer - and then the LORD puts to death the one liable to death, and each one receives his own share as is fitting for him, by measure, by weight, and by measure of capacity. And for this reason it is fitting to weep and mourn for all one's dead. "Why should a living man complain, a man for his own sins?" (Lamentations 3:39). (And more is written on this below under the entry "Nechamah" [consolation].)
Pele Yoetz 29:8: And even for an aged man, advanced in years, it is fitting to weep and mourn - and let him not rely on saying that he had already completed his term and reached his end, for one should nevertheless be concerned that perhaps he was fit to live some more days or years, and sin caused him to die before his time, and this is a distress in Heaven - for even one Jew who dies is greatly significant in the eyes of the Omnipresent, as our Sages, of blessed memory, expounded (Mechilta, Yitro, ch. 4) on the verse (Exodus 19:21), "lest many of them fall" - and all the more so if he is a worthy man, for there is reason to attribute his premature death to the sin of the generation, and great is the distress of Heaven, for the Shechinah is distressed over the death of the wicked, all the more so over the death of the righteous (Chagigah 15b) - for if the righteous man was lost, the world's righteous one was lost, and one was lost who would give peace of mind before the throne of His glory. Of such and similar matters, the living person shall take to heart to eulogize his own trouble and to weep for it with genuine weeping, over his own sins and over the distress of Heaven and the like - not an empty weeping of vanity and vexation of spirit - and through this he shall merit days in which there is delight, "and the LORD shall wipe away tears from all faces" (Isaiah 25:8), we shall attain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away (ibid. 35:10), and there shall be relief.
Pele Yoetz 30:1: Building - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Yevamot 63a): whoever engages in building becomes impoverished, may the Merciful One save us - for with all other expenses, a person knows how to calculate what he shall spend, and looks at his own pocket to see if he can afford it, and spends accordingly so as not to become impoverished; but not so one who engages in building - he plans to spend a hundred and it becomes an expense of two hundred, and once he has begun he cannot withdraw his hand, and thereby he may come to be impoverished. Therefore it is fitting for a man to first calculate whether he can spend double what they estimate that building requires before he engages in the building, and if not, he should not engage in it - for one must first look after his own livelihood, as people say: the shop builds the house, not the house the shop. And it would seem better for a person to buy a building already built, since that is something with a fixed price and can be bought cheaply and without trouble; however, according to the words of the Holy Zohar, Parashat Tazria (page 50), it is clear from the exposition that one should not buy a house built by an idolater even for free, for when an idolater builds his house he mentions over it the name of idolatry, and immediately the Other Side rests upon it and never departs from it, and whoever dwells there can be harmed. And this is the secret of the plague of leprosy that appeared in a house, so that they would demolish the house, its stones, and its timber. Not so when a Jew builds his house in righteousness - that is, that he be careful that it be built with permitted money, and at the laying of the foundation he clarify that his deeds are for the sake of Heaven and pour out his own words - and also, after the building is completed, he shall perform the dedication of the house with Torah study and pour out conversation (and I, the poor one, have already arranged an order of study and prayers, and appended them to my Beit Tefillati), and then holiness rests there. And regarding everything he spends, he shall say that it is for building a house to be settled for the service of God, blessed be He, and the more he mentions the Name of Heaven regarding the building, the better.
Pele Yoetz 30:2: And he should be very careful of the prohibition that many have trampled upon, allowing a gentile to build on the Sabbath or a festival or Chol HaMo'ed, for of such a case it is said (Jeremiah 22:13): "woe to him who builds his house without righteousness." And the halachic authorities wrote (Orach Chaim 244:3) that it is forbidden to enter that house, and those who stand in the breach are obligated to repair this breach if it is in their power to protest. And how good it would be, if the LORD has widened his boundary, to have a spacious place built specifically for himself alone, to seclude himself there for the service of his Maker, and also to build a house for hospitality to guests. And he should be careful to affix a kosher mezuzah on all the doorways. Whoever does these things - certainly the Shechinah dwells in his house, and the LORD shall guard his going out and his coming in, and he shall know that his tent is at peace. Therefore it is good for a man to build a building for himself rather than buy one already built, unless it happens that a worthy Jew who was careful about all these things sells his house.
Pele Yoetz 30:3: And in any case, he should not increase expenses on great buildings, stone construction, spacious upper rooms known and recognized [as luxurious], and the like, for all is vanity and vexation of spirit, and we are strangers, our days upon the earth are like a passing shadow (I Chronicles 29:15) - and it is better for him to spend those expenses to build himself a house that endures for the World to Come, for that is truly his home. And there is a story brought in the Yerushalmi (Shekalim, end of ch. 5) about two sages who were traveling from place to place, and there were in one place magnificent synagogues. One said to his fellow, how much money my ancestors spent in this place to build such magnificent synagogues! His fellow answered him, how many souls did your ancestors sink here! Were there no people to occupy themselves with Torah [instead]? - meaning, it would have been better for them to build the synagogue with light construction and give those expenses to Torah scholars. Take heed and consider - if this is said regarding the building of a synagogue, where there is an aspect of mitzvah in adorning the house of our God, what shall those who spend great sums to build large, fine houses answer on the day of reckoning, while the sages wander for bread?
Pele Yoetz 30:4: And they have already said (Rabbeinu Ovadiah of Bartenura, Avot 5:10) that the common people are called "people of the land" [am ha'aretz] because they occupy themselves with settling the land and building houses, for on the part of the Torah scholar, the world would remain desolate - for whoever has understanding would not want to waste time and consume his strength and his days building houses for a brief time, like a passing shadow, so that afterward others - his friends or his enemies or his wife's [second] husband - would dwell in them, while he goes to the grave, to a plot of earth a cubit by a cubit. But whoever has understanding shall turn to build for himself houses in the eternal and everlasting world through his good deeds, and shall build in this world only what is necessary, without which it is impossible to be settled for the service of God, blessed be His Name.
Pele Yoetz 30:5: And especially in the land of the [gentile] nations, if it is possible for a person to dwell in settled fashion by renting, it is better that he not build houses at all and not establish a permanent dwelling in an impure land - and this demonstrates faith in the redemption and awaiting salvation from day to day, as we have written in its place. But if the LORD has widened his boundary and he has abundant possessions, it is good for him to buy houses, courtyards, and shops, according to the blessing the LORD has given him, to rent out and collect rent, in order to fulfill the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Bava Metzia 42a): let a person always divide his money into three - one third in land, one third in merchandise, and one third in hand. And he can arrange that wealth and riches be in his house while his righteousness stands forever - for example, if he rents the house cheaply to a worthy poor man or to a Torah scholar. And it is fitting for a person to choose carefully to whom he rents the house, that it be a God-fearing man or a Torah scholar who shall study there and do good deeds there, in a manner that the Shechinah dwells in his house and his inheritance endures, in the manner of what is written (Proverbs 12:7): "the house of the righteous shall stand." Correspondingly, one who gives his house to an evil man - and the knowledge of opposites is one - behold, therefore, it is better to rent his house or his shop to a good, simple, and upright man even for half the rent, for his reward is better than the reward of money - he enjoys the fruits in this world while the principal remains for him in the World to Come; behold, his reward is with him and his recompense before him.
Pele Yoetz 31:1: Fleeing - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Avot 4:2): run to a mitzvah and flee from transgression. The matter of fleeing is to be concerned even about a remote concern, as they said, that one should flee a hundred gates of the permitted so as not to enter one gate of the forbidden. And they also said (Derech Eretz Zuta ch. 1; Sefer Chasidim): love the [word] "perhaps" - that regarding every place he wishes to go, he shall be concerned for his own soul that he might perhaps come to a prohibition. And likewise regarding every word he wishes to speak, he shall be very concerned that he might come to speak a forbidden word. And likewise regarding every deed he does. And he should flee from the permitted so as not to come to the forbidden, and should not go, nor speak, nor do anything except what is very necessary for the sake of a mitzvah or his own need, after clarifying with complete certainty that he cannot come to any hint of prohibition through it. This is pure fear of the LORD - happy is the man who fears the LORD. And one who guards himself greatly from every evil thing, the LORD too shall guard his soul from all evil, and the LORD shall complete [His protection] on his behalf, so that no mishap come from his own hand. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Chullin 10a): danger is more severe than prohibition. Therefore it is fitting to flee more and more from a place of concern and danger and from a place where harm is common, and one should not rely on a miracle, for perhaps no miracle shall be performed for him, and if a miracle is performed for him, they deduct from his merits, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 32a).
Pele Yoetz 31:2: And especially we, orphans of orphans, full of sins, must be concerned to flee greatly from danger, for Satan prosecutes at a time of danger. Go forth and learn from what is written (Deuteronomy 20:8): "who is the man who is fearful and fainthearted? Let him go and return to his house, lest he cause the heart of his brothers to melt like his own heart" - and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Menachot 36a): who is the man who is fearful - of the transgressions in his hand, for even one who spoke [an interruption] between putting on the tefillin of the hand and the tefillin of the head has committed a transgression, and he returns from the ranks of the army, even though it was a war of mitzvah - all the more so we, who from the sole of the foot to the head have no soundness in us (Isaiah 1:6), must guard ourselves very, very much and flee even from a remote concern of danger. And they have already said, "whoever gives his mother reason to rejoice, she shall not weep for him." And we find great men of the world who fled and were saved - "and Jacob fled" (Hosea 12:13), "and Moses fled" (Exodus 2:15), "and Elijah fled," and the like. And they said (Isaiah 26:20): "hide yourself for a brief moment, and you shall live for days everlasting" (and more is written on this under the entry "Shemirah" [guarding]).
Pele Yoetz 32:1: Choosing - It is fitting for a person to choose the good, both between two goods and between two lesser goods. Like a good merchant, who, when he comes to spend his money in merchandise, chooses the merchandise that has more profit in it, and in any case also buys a small amount of every kind of merchandise that he can, to give to any customer who asks - but the essential part of his trade shall be in that item which has more profit. So too the perfect man, when he comes to spend his free time, shall choose how to spend it on the most beneficial and most necessary thing. And likewise, in this manner, when he comes to study, he shall choose the most beneficial and most necessary study. And likewise, when he comes to spend his money on a mitzvah matter, he shall choose the mitzvah that is most important before the Omnipresent, and give to the best and most necessary cause. And in any case, let his hand be in everything, and let him hold on to this and not withdraw his hand from that either - but the essential thing he shall do is what is most pleasing and gives the most peace of mind before our Father in Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 32:2: And whoever does not know which way holds the light and which is the straight path a person should choose, let him go to a sage and let him teach him, and let him be guided by his counsel. Only regarding this must he understand of his own mind, or the sage shall tell him, that he need not rely on others - for the greatest of charities is to support those who study Torah; it is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it, and there is no better trait than this. And likewise regarding evil, if he is greatly forced by circumstances to do something evil, let him choose the lesser evil, for whatever he minimizes, his punishment shall be lightened and shall testify to his being under duress - but if he adds to what is required by necessity, his very duress shall be counted to him as willful, and God shall bring everything into judgment, for there is evidence that his own soul desired to do that scheme. And conversely, if he minimizes in matters of prohibition, there is evidence that he fears God, and "the Merciful One exempts him" as one under duress.
Pele Yoetz 33:1: Young Man - It is written (Ecclesiastes 12:1): "remember your Creator in the days of your youth" - for then is the most fitting time to serve his Creator, for as a man his strength and his vigor belong to the Torah, to labor with all his might in depth of study and to make nights like days with little sleep, and then he is free, without so many disturbances of the times, and his mind is clear and settled, and he can understand, become wise, listen, learn, and teach. And since he does not have so many disturbances, especially if he is dependent on his father's table and has no worries at all, everything he learns is recorded in his memory - as our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Avot 4:20): one who learns Torah as a child, to what is he compared? To ink written on new paper, which is clear and lasting. And this Torah [learned in youth] shall stand by Torah scholars in their old age, when their minds are more settled - for the Torah of youth is the leaven in the dough, the cornerstone.
Pele Yoetz 33:2: Behold, therefore, precious young men who occupy yourselves with Torah, have mercy on this precious time, and do not lose from it even the time it takes to say a word, and gird yourselves with strength to labor in Torah with all your strength - for of this time it is said (Ecclesiastes... [an obscure allusion]): "you have labored and not found - do not believe it" [i.e. of Torah study, effort is never in vain]. And even though all the days of a person's life, time is precious, and every moment lost is a great, irretrievable loss, this particular time is the choicest of times, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 152a): youth is a crown of roses. And it is fitting to have mercy upon it and upon the honor of one's Maker all the more.
Pele Yoetz 33:3: And likewise regarding the service of God, blessed be He, youth is the fitting time to run like a deer, be swift as an eagle, and mighty as a lion to do the will of our Father in Heaven, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Avot 3:12): be gentle-headed and pleasant to youth. And in the days of youth, whatever a man desires he can do, for his strength is the strength of stones. And likewise regarding repentance, youth is the fitting time to fulfill the ways of repentance, for he can afflict his body with fasts and mortifications, and rise before the night watches to pour out his conversation, seeking forgiveness, and other such ways of repentance. And all the good that a person does in the time of his youth, holding fast to the ways of repentance and abstinence, is more esteemed and pleasing before the Omnipresent, since he has the seething of the blood and his inclination overpowers him, and he is a mighty man who conquers his inclination - as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Avodah Zarah 19a): "happy is the man who fears the LORD" (Psalms 112:1) - happy is he who repents while he is [still] a man, meaning in the time of his youth - and since he accustoms himself to walk in the way of the good, so he shall continue to do, and so he shall add.
Pele Yoetz 33:4: Correspondingly, whoever walks in an evil way adds transgression to his sin day by day, in the manner of the evil inclination, which today tells him to do this and tomorrow tells him to do that, and so on. And likewise is the way of a man - that according to the way he accustoms himself in the days of his youth, even when he grows old he shall not depart from it. And further, since he has not taken for himself a path of walking in the way of the good from the time of his youth, if his eyes open in the days of his old age, repentance shall be difficult for him in the days of his old age. And this is how I explain their saying, of blessed memory (Shabbat 152a): "childhood and youth are vanity" (Ecclesiastes 11:10) - things a person does in his childhood blacken his face in his old age. And Rashi explained this as referring to excessive marital relations - but this too can be said in their words, that if he is not careful in his youth to walk in the way of the good, he must blacken his face in his old age to correct what he has perverted.
Pele Yoetz 33:5: And in any case, even if he did not take it to heart from the beginning to serve God's service properly day by day, let him gird his loins like a mighty man for Torah, for service, and for repentance, and let him say: I shall repent today, lest I die tomorrow - for death does not delay, small and great are there [in the grave] alike, and even if he should live many more years, he shall never again be a young man as he is today - and if not now, when? Perhaps tomorrow he shall not be able to do as he can today, and even if he can, it is enough for today that he discharge his obligation and atone for himself, for this day passes and shall not return, and how shall he repair this day [otherwise]? Therefore let him swiftly find an escape for himself, one day before, and find thereby his own redemption.
Pele Yoetz 33:6: But now, not so - many young men among the people follow the counsel of their own inclination, and so they advise one another, saying (Ecclesiastes 11:9): "rejoice, young man, in your youth," for youth comes but once. "And how shall it be known that we are young men? Come, let us drink our fill of love until morning, let us delight ourselves with love, and let us make nights like days." "A time to laugh and a time to drink, a time to sing and a time to dance" (Ecclesiastes 3:5-6, adapted) - and such other human pleasures, which are vanity and vexation of spirit, consuming a person from soul to flesh, for the expense multiplies and the body is oppressed and afflicted, and sins and guilt increase, and "they do not regard the work of the LORD" (Isaiah 5:12), for they lose blessings, the recitation of Shema, and prayers, and many such evils, as is publicly known to anyone whose eyes are not sealed. Therefore, whoever is a man who desires life, who is a Jew and believes in our holy Torah and in the words of our holy Rabbis, of blessed memory - if sinners entice him, let him not consent, and let him remember always that God shall bring every hidden thing into judgment, and let him fear the LORD from his youth - and behold, the LORD stands over him, He shall be his help, for whoever comes to purify himself is helped [from Heaven].
Pele Yoetz 34:1: Meat - In most places meat is scarce, and especially when many set their eyes on a fine portion and many grab hold of one piece of meat, this one pulling toward himself and that one pulling toward himself, increasing dispute, and in the end "whoever is stronger prevails." But in this the perfect and modest men are distinguished, who withdraw their hands and are content with whatever comes to them, or who do not take any meat at all from the butcher shop so as not to cause dispute, but rather take fowl for themselves, for dispute is hated. And regardless, it is better if it is possible for him to always eat fowl, for he is thereby saved from many stumbling blocks, as I shall write below under the entry "Shochet" [ritual slaughterer].
Pele Yoetz 34:2: And whoever can afford to be pious with his Maker should eat meat only from Sabbath to Sabbath and on days when supplications [Tachanun] are not said - for it is written in Sefer Chesed LeAvraham, in these words: know that the punishment of the beating of the grave comes only because of the joy a person indulges in at a time when it is not fitting, and there is no joy except with meat and wine, and all the days permitted for [prostration in] falling on one's face are not days of joy, and therefore eating meat and drinking wine are forbidden on them - unless he takes the meat and wine for the sake of the Sabbath, or they are the permitted leftovers of the Sabbath, which are permitted; but otherwise they are forbidden, and he is punished for them with the beating of the grave - see there. But only one from a family of the healthy can fulfill this. And now we have an excuse, saying that this is beyond our strength - so its law is: if we are careful not to increase in celebrations and rejoicing, frivolous merriment, and optional feasts, but rather eat to satisfy our own souls with good intention, and let all our deeds be for the sake of Heaven - perhaps God shall take counsel for us and the LORD shall not count it as sin for us. And it is good for a man to fulfill what he can easily fulfill of the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, who said on the verse (Exodus 16:8), "when the LORD gives you meat to eat in the evening and bread in the morning" - the Torah taught proper conduct, that a person should eat meat only at night (Yoma 75b). And everything is according to what kind of person he is - let him conduct his affairs with judgment and eat less than what he has and less than his full satiety, and not increase in meat, and through this even his own flesh shall dwell securely.
Pele Yoetz 35:1: Good Tidings - If he knows good tidings for his fellow, let him hasten to bring them to him, and his soul shall live because of him, and it shall be counted a mitzvah for him - all the more so for a righteous man, for whoever causes his spirit to revive shall have life added to him. Go forth and learn from Serach the daughter of Asher, who, because she brought Jacob the tidings that Joseph was alive, merited to enter the Garden of Eden alive (see Targum Yonatan, Genesis 46:17; Derech Eretz Zuta, ch. 1). And this is included in the mitzvah of acts of kindness. And just as regarding charity they said (Bava Metzia 71a), "your own poor take precedence," so is the matter regarding acts of kindness. And it is not good what the lazy ones do, who, when traveling on the roads, do not write to their relatives and household members to inform them of their well-being, and their souls melt in distress according to the abundance of their love, as people say: what one thinks is for a friend may reach an enemy [i.e. bad consequences from negligence] - certainly they are destined to give an account. And a man who is good shall have his hand write in every direction and by many routes, so that his letters reach them, if not all of them, at least some of them, and shall mention the residents of his own city who are with him. And it is a mitzvah upon everyone to whom a letter reaches to take the trouble, with body and money, to send it, hasten it, and get it to the hand of its owner, and it shall be counted as a great mitzvah for him, for sometimes he thereby restores a soul, and he fulfills several mitzvot - acts of kindness and the mitzvah of "love your fellow as yourself" - and is a servant who benefits by gladdening wretched hearts and reviving downtrodden hearts, and shall carry a blessing from the LORD and from men.
Pele Yoetz 35:2: Correspondingly, bad news should not be heard from his mouth - for our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Pesachim 103b) that of one who brings bad news, Scripture says (Proverbs 10:18), "he who spreads slander is a fool." And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Megillah 15a) that even one who sends to his fellow to know something and to answer him a matter - if the answer is bad, he should not answer him at all, for one does not respond regarding a mishap, as we find with Hatach, who did not want to tell Mordechai Esther's words [directly, out of concern]. And if sometimes he is forced to tell his fellow some bad news because of some need of the hour, let him tell him by hint, in a manner that he understands on his own, or tell him through a gentile, and not send it through another Jew - for they said (Shabbat 31a): that which is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow - unless he wants him not to know suddenly, in which case a wise-hearted person is needed to tell the matter in a proper order.
Pele Yoetz 36:1: Living Creatures - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 128b): the suffering of living creatures is a matter of Torah law. And one must feed them before eating himself, as they learned (Berachot 40a) from the verse (Deuteronomy 11:15), "and I shall give grass in your field for your cattle, and afterward you shall eat" - for they depend on him, and he depends on the One who spoke and the world came into being. And it was already told, an incident in the time of the Ari, of blessed memory, about a man who was punished with the death of his children because of the suffering of small chicks that had a basket to climb up after hatching, and his wife, even unknowingly, removed the basket, and he was punished. Let the wise man hear and increase learning (Proverbs 1:5) to fulfill the testament of Rabbi Yehudah HeChasid not to raise chicks at all, for one cannot stand guard so that they suffer no distress, and mostly they do not succeed - most of them die from falling or become food for cats and mice and the like, and this is distress to the soul; therefore their absence is preferable. And it is possible for the world to be sustained through the gentiles, for it is fitting for them to occupy themselves with the settlement of this world. And likewise it is not good for a man to raise fowl, but rather, when he needs one, he should buy it and have it slaughtered - and if he cannot find one at every time and needs to have them ready at hand, he should be very careful and instruct his children and all the members of his household to be careful to give them their food at its proper time, for their sustenance is upon him and their punishment is severe - and especially if they are confined in a cage, he must have extra mercy on them and feed them promptly, so as not to stumble into the sin of causing suffering to living creatures.
Pele Yoetz 36:2: And from this one should learn regarding all who are dependent upon him, such as the members of his household and his servants and the community's servants, who are like chickens confined in a coop, whose eyes are turned toward the master of the house - one must be diligent and press himself to give them their food, sufficient for their need, at its proper time, before he eats himself. And with the measure a person measures, they measure to him (Megillah 12b, Sotah 8b) - the LORD too shall give him his sufficient need in its proper time. And behold, the halachic authorities disagreed (Birkei Yosef 372) as to whether the suffering of human beings is a matter of Torah law like the suffering of living creatures - for some say it is all the more so, and some say that this prohibition is stated by Torah law only regarding living creatures who have no understanding to bear and accept [their situation], but in any case, hold that the suffering of small children who have no understanding is a matter of Torah law, and one must be very careful not to cause them distress (as we have written under the entry "Yonek" [nursing infant]), and not to cause distress to any person, for "God shall bring every hidden thing into judgment" (Ecclesiastes 12:14) - and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Chagigah 5a) that even one who killed a louse or spat in front of his fellow, causing him to feel disgust and distress, is destined to give an account, even though he did not intend to cause him distress. Therefore let a man tremble and be seized [with fear], and do whatever is in his power to do so that the spirit of his fellow creatures be at ease with him - and even if it is decreed upon a person that he shall suffer, let it not be through his own deed that the one who falls falls. (And more is written under the entry "Rachamanut" [compassion].)
Pele Yoetz 37:1: First Fruits - Bikkurim [first fruits] is one of the 613 mitzvot that was observed while the Temple stood. And there is an equivalent to it in this time, for they said (Ketubot 105b): whoever brings a gift to a Torah scholar is as though he had offered the first fruits. And we have already written elsewhere that whoever says his heart aches because, due to our sins, the Temple was destroyed and we cannot fulfill the mitzvot that were observed while the Temple stood, shall know whether these words are sincere by whether he fulfills the mitzvot that are their equivalent, and does whatever is in his power to do. And it is fitting for a man and a woman whose hearts move them to give their Maker peace of mind, to set aside the first and best of everything in their house - of the grain, wine, and oil they buy, and all household matters they purchase - to first set aside their portion for the LORD and give it to those who labor in Torah or to poor people of good family. And it is known that the virtue of charity is great when giving household items whose benefit is close at hand [i.e. immediately useful] (Ta'anit 23b), and this is the equivalent of the mitzvah of first fruits and helps leave a blessing in their storehouse. And it is included in the mitzvah of first fruits that, if one wishes to divide his sons - that some of them or one of them have his portion among those who sit in the study house, and some of them or one of them be occupied in commerce, in order to support those who study so that they can stand guard over the Torah - he should choose and strive that his firstborn son be dedicated to the LORD. And support for this is found in "sanctify to Me every firstborn" (Exodus 13:2) - unless the other son is sharper, more diligent, and more capable, and the firstborn is not fit to be a Torah scholar, in which case what can be done - let the better one come regardless. But he should strive with all his strength to first bring merit to the firstborn, that he be the Torah scholar - for besides its being fitting to offer to the LORD the first fruits as long as there is good reason, if the younger son becomes the Torah scholar he shall be honored by people more than his elder brother, and the elder brother too is obligated to honor his younger brother who is a Torah scholar - and jealousy as harsh as Sheol is difficult and brings hatred and rivalry - but when the firstborn is the Torah scholar, everything comes out properly, like a sapphire and diamond set together, and each man shall come to his place in peace.
Pele Yoetz 38:1: Arbitrators - It is good to judge between a man and his fellow, especially in a place where there is no halachic authority - and even in a place where there is a halachic authority, for any particularly difficult matter it is better that it be judged through arbitrators: this party chooses one or two arbitrators, and that party chooses one or two arbitrators, and the two sides together choose yet another - for through this a proper judgment shall emerge, since each side searches for merit for the one who chose him, and they discuss the matter, and the middle arbitrator decides between them. And it is fitting for the arbitrators not to seek to find merit for the one who chose them through vain and misleading claims, and not to hold fast to their own claims, but rather this shall be their glory - that they acknowledge the truth and judge a righteous judgment, and through this they shall demonstrate their righteousness, that they show no favoritism to the one who chose them - for even though he is their beloved, truth is more beloved still. And even if they stand by their own opinion according to their own understanding, and the judgment is decided against the one who chose them because of the deciding vote of the middle arbitrator, it is forbidden to reveal this to the litigant and say, "I would acquit you, but what can I do since my colleagues outvoted me" - for one who does this transgresses "you shall not go about as a talebearer among your people" (Leviticus 19:16), as our Sages, of blessed memory, expounded (Sanhedrin 31a). Therefore, in every kind of tribunal that is convened, whether of the city's sages or its notables or arbitrators and the like, after the judgment is rendered it is fitting for the one who voted to acquit to retract and say to the liable party, "So-and-so, you are liable, for this is how the judgment came out among us according to what is right" - and thereby the liable party shall accept the judgment with a pleasant countenance and not resist, and shall not come to suspect [foul play] upon seeing his arbitrators embrace him, saying truly, "truth guides his way," and if they take from him his cloak by law, let him sing and go on his way (Sanhedrin 7a), and each man shall come to his place in peace.
Pele Yoetz 38:2: But if the arbitrators search greatly for merit for the one who chose them, to the point of calling evil good, "making the crooked straight" (Isaiah 40:4) and twisting the straight, behold, they have stumbled into the sin of one who perverts justice, who is called hated, detestable, banned, an injustice, an abomination, and acquires for himself a bad name - for the matters are recognizable, and it is easy for the discerning to know that he understands the truth but suppresses it deliberately and wants to cover the sun with a sieve, and it is found that he makes himself wicked before the creatures, showing favoritism in judgment. But whoever judges a true judgment truly, even against the one who chose him for his own benefit, all who hear of it shall come and declare his righteousness. And if the arbitrators are not chosen by both sides, but rather chosen from the community, and it happens that a man comes before them for judgment who has a relationship or partnership with one of the arbitrating judges, it is fitting for the relative to search as far as his own hand can reach to find fault with his relative if he can find it honestly - and if he can find only merit, let him remain silent and not speak either for good or for bad, so that a listener not suspect him of showing favoritism to his relative, and one should be concerned lest the affection of his relationship cover his fault and show only his merit - and it has already been noted as a sign: every affliction a person sees except his own affliction, and not even the afflictions of his relatives (see Midrash Shmuel 1:7; Nega'im 2:5) - and all such matters require understanding and wisdom to remain clean before the LORD and before Israel.
Pele Yoetz 39:1: Pure of Heart - It is written (Psalms 24:3-4): "who shall ascend the mountain of the LORD, and who shall stand in His holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart." And the explanation of "pure of heart" is that he not sin in his heart by thinking evil and forbidden thoughts, especially during prayer and Torah study - for the heart is the King's palace, and if he brings forbidden thoughts into it, it is as though he brings an idol into the palace, God forbid. And not only that, but even to let one's heart wander idly is forbidden, as our Sages, of blessed memory, expounded on the verse (Leviticus 19:4), "do not turn to idols [elilim]" - do not turn away to your own devices [midato'atkhem, a wordplay] (Shabbat 149a). And for this reason they forbade gazing at [immodest] images, because it causes one's mind to wander, and from this we learn regarding all kinds of laughter and levity, which are forbidden for this reason, as explained in the books. And it does not suffice merely to remember the LORD, but one must cling to Him with desire and love, sparks of the flame of the fire of the LORD - and this is difficult service, especially for us, whose coarse matter, the loss of purity, and dwelling in the impure land of the gentiles, and the intensified exile of body and soul, and our many disturbances from the incidents of the time, have all been our undoing - and our sins too withhold good from us. But in any case, an obligation rests upon us to strengthen ourselves with all our might to push away from ourselves, with both hands, every kind of strange thought and evil rumination, and let his heart cry out to Him like a father, saying: "save me from the mire, and let me not sink" (Psalms 69:15). "Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me" (ibid. 51:12). "Restore to me the joy of Your salvation," and so on (ibid. verse 14). And let him strive with all his strength, at every time and every moment, to exchange strange ruminations and evil thoughts for good ones - and if his heart cannot withstand his inclination before it, let him call out for help, and say with a full mouth in a loud voice, "I hate vain thoughts" (ibid. 119:113), and speak such verses and supplications, and the LORD shall be his help to save him from his inclination and enable him to cling to his Maker.
Pele Yoetz 40:1: Clarifying - It is known that all of man's coming into this world and all the exiles we suffer are all in order to clarify the sparks of holiness that were scattered among the husks, and this is the entire fruit of our prayers, our mitzvot, and our studies - and one must have this intention. And likewise one must have this intention in every eating and drinking and every hardship and trouble and wandering and affliction that Israel suffers in the exiles - all of it is a great benefit for this purpose, and therefore one must accept them with love, for everything is as nothing compared to love of the Creator and compared to giving peace of mind before the throne of His glory, and there is no greater peace of mind before Him than this - that all the souls and the sparks of holiness are a portion of God from above. And to what is the matter comparable? To a king whose beloved sons went into captivity at the hand of an adversary and dwell in a narrow place of darkness and the shadow of death, causing the king great distress - and whoever redeems the king's sons performs a great kindness for the king, and the king shall repay him his recompense. So is this matter, by way of comparison, insofar as we can grasp it. And there is still more to say on ancient matters concerning God.
